Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine. Born and raised in New York City, USA, he studied at the New York University School of Medicine and later conducted his landmark vaccine research at the University of Pittsburgh.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians such as Beethoven and Mozart spent their prime years working there. The city center features the towering Gothic spire of St. Stephen's Cathedral.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. It is located on the eastern coast of the island of Zealand. The city is a major center of culture, business, media, and science, and is the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Sydney Opera House.

Title: Poland
Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a country located in Central Europe. It is divided into 16 administrative provinces and shares borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia. The country's southern border is defined by the rugged Sudeten and Carpathian mountain ranges.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Kapuskasing
Kapuskasing is a town on the Kapuskasing River in the Cochrane District of Northern Ontario, Canada. Founded in the early 20th century as a water stop along the National Transcontinental Railway, it relies heavily on the forestry and paper industries. It is the birthplace of several notable Canadian figures.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was hosted by Mexico. The tournament was defined by the phenomenal performance of the team captain who scored the "Hand of God" goal, leading his nation to a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Jurassic Park (film)
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. It was an enormous critical and commercial success, shattering box office records to become the highest-grossing film of 1993. The film's groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs were brought to life based on a highly successful techno-thriller novel written by Michael Crichton.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: Rocky Mountains
The Rocky Mountains are a major mountain range in western North America. They stretch more than 3,000 miles from the northernmost part of British Columbia, in western Canada, to New Mexico in the Southwestern United States, providing a massive continental divide.

Title: 1797 in Great Britain
The year 1797 in Great Britain was marked by several significant historical events, including the Battle of Cape St Vincent and widespread naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. It was also a notable year in literature, serving as the birth year of several prominent literary figures, including the future creator of a legendary literary monster.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Because of its remote location, it was one of the last lands to be settled by humans and is famous for its unique birdlife, such as the flightless kiwi. Its national capital is Wellington, located on the North Island.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: Inactivated Polio Vaccine
The first successful polio vaccine was an inactivated version developed in the early 1950s. Requiring an injection, it was declared safe and effective after a massive nationwide field trial in 1955. The medical researcher who led its creation became an international hero but chose not to patent his formula.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. The country features vast geographical diversity, spanning from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Its highest physical elevation is the peak of Denali in Alaska.

Title: Eleanor of Aquitaine
Eleanor of Aquitaine was one of the most powerful and wealthy women in western Europe during the High Middle Ages. She was Queen of France and later Queen of England. She was the mother of both Richard the Lionheart and King John, predating the turbulent barons' revolt.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is bordered by New York, the Atlantic Ocean, Delaware, and Pennsylvania. Despite being one of the smallest states by land area, it is highly populated. Its state capital is Trenton.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Seaborg was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, Michigan, and later spent most of his career at UC Berkeley.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in middle and high schools across the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot is loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1949. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Zhytomyr
Zhytomyr is a city in the north of the western half of Ukraine. It is the administrative center of Zhytomyr Oblast. A historic city, it was a major transport hub linking Kiev with points west. It proudly serves as the birthplace of the chief designer of the early Soviet space program.

Title: Trinity Test
The Trinity test was the world's first successful detonation of a nuclear weapon. Conducted by the United States Army on July 16, 1945, as part of the Manhattan Project, the test involved an implosion-design plutonium device. The monumental explosion took place in the Jornada del Muerto desert region of New Mexico.

Query: What is the name of the river that flows through the birth city of the composer who wrote the '1812 Overture'?

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: Mount Narodnaya
Mount Narodnaya is the highest peak of the Ural Mountains in Russia. Its elevation is 1,894 metres (6,214 ft). The mountain is located in the Research Range, on the border between the Komi Republic and Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, standing as the apex of the massive intercontinental divide.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Kapuskasing
Kapuskasing is a town on the Kapuskasing River in the Cochrane District of Northern Ontario, Canada. Founded in the early 20th century as a water stop along the National Transcontinental Railway, it relies heavily on the forestry and paper industries. It is the birthplace of several notable Canadian figures.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a Russian composer, pianist, and conductor, later of French and American citizenship. He is widely considered one of the most important and influential composers of the 20th century. Stravinsky composed the revolutionary score for "The Rite of Spring". He was born in the resort town of Oranienbaum, Russia.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine and part of the Carpathian Mountains. The mountain is situated in the Eastern Beskids, in the Chornohora region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr. He received the honor "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." Bohr's atomic model revolutionized the understanding of subatomic structures and quantum mechanics.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era, a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom. She was the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II.

Title: America's First Satellite
Following the unexpected success of the Soviet space program, the United States scrambled to catch up. A few months later, in early 1958, the US successfully launched Explorer 1, its first artificial satellite. This mission famously led to the discovery of the Van Allen radiation belts surrounding Earth.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. It was the epicenter of the French Revolution and the seat of power for the First French Empire. Napoleon Bonaparte oversaw many architectural transformations in the city, including the commissioning of the Arc de Triomphe.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, and a historic landmark in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as the Louvre castle in the late 12th to 13th century under Philip II.

Title: Modest Mussorgsky
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five". He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period, striving to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity. Mussorgsky was born in Toropets, located in the western region of the Russian Empire.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. The tournament was hosted by Mexico, which stepped in after the original host, Colombia, withdrew due to financial reasons. Argentina won the tournament, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Query: Who was the prime minister of the United Kingdom when the country where the inventor of the first practical telephone was born achieved full legislative independence?

Title: Rocky Mountains
The Rocky Mountains are a major mountain range in western North America. They stretch more than 3,000 miles from the northernmost part of British Columbia, in western Canada, to New Mexico in the Southwestern United States, providing a massive continental divide.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne. It opens with a dense introductory chapter titled "The Custom-House."

Title: Björn Borg
Björn Borg is a former world No. 1 tennis player widely considered one of the greatest in the history of the sport. He was famous for his unmatched dominance on both grass and clay courts during the late 1970s. Borg was born and raised in the country of Sweden.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State populated by genetically engineered citizens arranged in a strict social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive technological advancements in reproductive biology and behavioral conditioning. It is considered one of the definitive dystopian works of the 20th century.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Ramsay MacDonald
James Ramsay MacDonald was a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. He was a founder of the Labour Party and led governments during periods of severe economic crisis. He was serving as Prime Minister in December 1931 when the British Parliament passed the landmark Statute of Westminster.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. Born in December 1822 in Dole, France, his research practically eliminated several diseases. He developed the first vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: Rosalind Franklin
Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to the understanding of the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, and coal. Her famous Photo 51 was critical in determining the double helix structure of DNA, though she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

Title: The Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a massive, secretive research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. Led by the United States with support from the UK and Canada, the project's scientific research was directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at the Los Alamos Laboratory.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The Irish Sea lies northwest of England and the Celtic Sea to the southwest. Historically, its territory served as the bloody battleground for the Wars of the Roses, including the decisive clash at Bosworth Field.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Founded in 1960 by a pioneering virologist, it is renowned for its striking modernist architecture and its massive contributions to molecular biology and genetics.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and a member of Young Bosnia, an organization seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir apparent and his wife by firing a pistol at their open car as it stalled in the streets of Sarajevo.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, ending his reign as Emperor of the French.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. It boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center dominated by its massive central cathedral, attracting millions of tourists each year.

Title: First Practical Telephone
The invention of the first practical telephone was a watershed moment in human engineering, transforming global communication forever. The device was successfully patented in the United States in March 1876. The inventor, who spent much of his adult life working in America, was born and educated in Edinburgh, Scotland.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: The Greatest (Boxer)
Widely regarded as one of the most significant sports figures of the 20th century, the boxer known universally as "The Greatest" was a three-time heavyweight champion. Known for his legendary trash talk and political activism, he famously refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, sound recording, and motion pictures. Born in Ohio, he built a massive industrial research facility that pioneered the process of organized collaborative invention.

Title: Rhine River
The Rhine is one of the major European rivers, flowing from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea coast in the Netherlands. It serves as a vital navigable waterway and forms part of the borders between Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, France, and Germany.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: French Revolution
The French Revolution was a period of radical political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789. It resulted in the overthrow of the monarchy, the establishment of a republic, and extensive social upheaval. The era is notable for the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were executed.

Title: Alexander Graham Bell
Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor, scientist, and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847, his family later emigrated to Canada before he established his professional research career in Boston, Massachusetts.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Statute of Westminster 1931
The Statute of Westminster 1931 was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that established the status of legislative independence for the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. This historic statute granted full legislative sovereignty to several nations, including Canada, South Africa, and the United Kingdom's neighbor, the Irish Free State.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has long been a global center of art, science, and philosophy. As a founding member of the European Union and the Eurozone, the official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French Franc.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. The building was designed in the style of high-tech architecture by the architectural team of Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. In 1911, he proposed his own model of the atom after the famous gold foil experiment, which proved that the atom has a tiny, dense nucleus. He was a mentor to many pioneering physicists of the 20th century.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Query: What is the official currency of the country where the real-time operating system used on NASA's Mars Perseverance rover was created?

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Euro
The Euro (symbol: €; code: EUR) is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: Renzo Piano
Renzo Piano is an Italian architect known for his high-tech public spaces. He gained international fame for co-designing the Centre Pompidou in Paris, a building featuring its structural and mechanical systems exposed on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London, currently the tallest building in the UK.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA. Formally launched in 1990, it revolutionized the field of genetics. A working draft of the genome was proudly announced to the world in 2000.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. She was not the ruler of the Austrian territories where early geneticists were born.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. The rover's sophisticated payload, autonomous navigation systems, and mission-critical flight computers are managed by a commercial, high-reliability real-time operating system.

Title: Falklands War
The Falklands War was a ten-week undeclared war between Argentina and the United Kingdom in 1982 over two British dependent territories in the South Atlantic: the Falkland Islands and its territorial dependency, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The conflict began on April 2, 1982, with an Argentine invasion.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America, consisting of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. It is a global leader in technological innovation, aerospace engineering, and software development. The official currency of the nation is the United States dollar ($).

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, securing the Physics prize in 1903. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, before moving to the French capital to advance her education.

Title: Kobe Bryant
Kobe Bryant was an American professional basketball player who spent his entire 20-year career with the Los Angeles Lakers. He entered the NBA directly from high school, famously bypassing the traditional college basketball route, and went on to win five NBA championships.

Title: Wheeler Peak
Wheeler Peak is the highest natural point in the U.S. state of New Mexico. Standing at an elevation of 13,167 feet (4,013 m), it is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the southernmost subrange of the Rocky Mountains. It is a highly popular destination for advanced alpine hikers and climbers.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, which are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The five main moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Out of all these orbiting satellites, the largest and most massive is the heavily cratered moon known as Titania.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their final years there. The city's geography is famously defined by the massive Danube River that flows directly through it.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions.
